OpenAI Codex CLI vs Claude Code: Which Terminal Coding Agent Should You Use? (2026)
Checked September 26, 2026 against OpenAI's Codex docs and GitHub

Here is the short answer. Both are terminal-based AI coding agents that read your codebase, write and edit files, run commands, and iterate until a task is done. Both start at $20 a month. Their feature lists now overlap more than they differ: OpenAI's docs cover subagents, MCP, hooks, skills, plugins, IDE integrations and a desktop app for OpenAI Codex CLI, and Claude Code (Anthropic) has its own version of each. The differences that remain are the models behind them (OpenAI's GPT-6 family for Codex, Anthropic's Claude models for Claude Code), the license (Codex CLI is open source under Apache-2.0, Claude Code is proprietary), and which subscription your team already pays for. Neither one is the objectively "better" agent, and the right pick depends on which ecosystem your team already lives in.

We run Claude Code daily in production for client work, so read this with that in mind. We have tried to write the fair version of this comparison rather than the marketing version: verified facts, no invented benchmark numbers, and an honest list of where each tool has the edge.
What is OpenAI Codex CLI?

Codex CLI is OpenAI's official coding agent that runs locally in your terminal. You describe a task in plain language, and Codex reads the relevant files, makes edits, and executes commands, while you control how much it can do without asking first.

OpenAI documents four install paths: a standalone script for macOS and Linux (curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh), a PowerShell script for Windows, npm (npm install -g @openai/codex), and Homebrew (brew install --cask codex). The CLI is open source under the Apache-2.0 license, written mostly in Rust, with the code on GitHub. The latest release on September 26, 2026 was 0.157.1.
Key properties:

Model. If you do not set a model, Codex uses a recommended one. OpenAI currently recommends GPT-6 Sol (gpt-6-sol) for complex coding and agentic work and GPT-6 Luna (gpt-6-luna) for focused, repeatable tasks, with GPT-6 Astra as its most capable model for the hardest end-to-end work. Switch with /model in a session or codex --model gpt-6-sol at launch. GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna remain available during the rollout, and GPT-5.5 retires from Codex with ChatGPT sign-in on October 14, 2026.

Authentication. You can sign in with your ChatGPT account (Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, or Enterprise) to use your plan's included usage, or sign in with an API key and pay standard OpenAI API rates. API-key sign-in has no cloud features such as GitHub code review or Slack.

Permissions. Two layers work together. A sandbox mode (read-only, workspace-write, or danger-full-access) sets what Codex can technically touch, and an approval policy (such as on-request or never) sets when it must stop and ask. By default the local sandbox keeps network access off and limits writes to the active workspace. The /permissions command changes this mid-session.
Extensibility. AGENTS.md project instructions, skills, plugins, MCP servers (codex mcp), hooks, and subagents.

Beyond the terminal. An IDE extension for VS Code and compatible editors (Xcode and JetBrains have their own integrations), the ChatGPT desktop app (codex app), Codex cloud on the web, iOS, a Codex SDK, and a GitHub Action.

Key takeaway: Codex CLI is OpenAI's terminal coding agent, billed either through your existing ChatGPT plan or pay-as-you-go API usage, open source, and built around OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol, Luna and Astra models.

What is Claude Code?

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads your codebase, writes and edits files, runs commands and tests, and iterates on failures across multiple files until a task is complete. It runs in the terminal, as IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains), as a desktop app, and in the browser at claude.ai/code.

Installation on macOS, Linux, and WSL is a single script (curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash), with Homebrew, WinGet, and native Windows PowerShell installers also documented at code.claude.com.
Key properties:

Model. Claude Code runs on Anthropic's Claude models; most surfaces require a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console (API) account, and the terminal CLI and VS Code extension also support select third-party model providers.

Customization layer. CLAUDE.md files hold project-level instructions, and Claude Code also builds its own auto memory as it works. Skills package repeatable workflows, and hooks run shell commands around Claude Code's actions.
Scale. You can spawn multiple Claude Code subagents that work on different parts of a task at once, run background agents in parallel, or build fully custom agents with the Agent SDK.
MCP. The Model Context Protocol connects Claude Code to external tools and data, Google Drive, Jira, Slack, or your own custom servers.
Beyond the terminal. Claude Code also runs as a desktop app, on the web, via a mobile app, through Slack, and on a schedule through Routines or /loop.

Key takeaway: Claude Code is Anthropic's terminal coding agent, included in Claude subscriptions or billed via API, with auto memory, chat-platform integrations and scheduled Routines on top of the terminal loop.

How do OpenAI Codex CLI and Claude Code actually compare?

A few things stand out once you strip the marketing away. Both tools charge the same $20 a month for their entry-level individual plan, and both put their top individual tier at "from $100/month" with the same 5x/20x usage-multiplier structure. Neither company has published head-to-head benchmark numbers we would trust enough to repeat here, so we are not going to invent a coding-accuracy score for either one. The feature lists also overlap heavily now: OpenAI's Codex docs cover hooks, MCP, subagents, skills, plugins and an SDK, which this comparison used to list as Claude Code advantages. What still separates them is the model family, the license, the billing path, and how each tool expresses permissions.
When does OpenAI Codex CLI make more sense?

Your team already runs on ChatGPT. If Plus, Pro, or Business seats already exist across your org, Codex CLI usage rides on a subscription you are already paying for, with no separate procurement conversation.

You want an open-source client. Codex CLI is Apache-2.0, so teams that want to inspect, fork, or extend the client itself have a lower barrier than with a proprietary tool. OpenAI's docs also say Codex can point at other model providers that support the Chat Completions or Responses APIs.
You want cloud offload for long tasks. Codex cloud runs tasks in isolated OpenAI-managed containers, and codex cloud lets you submit work from the terminal and apply the result locally later.

You are already deep in the OpenAI ecosystem. If your other tooling, evals, and internal scripts already assume OpenAI's API and model family, staying in one vendor's stack reduces integration overhead.
When does Claude Code make more sense?
You want Anthropic's models. Claude Code is built around Claude, so if your team already prefers Claude's output on your codebase, this is the direct path to it.
You want the customization layer to compound. CLAUDE.md, auto memory, skills, and hooks stack together, so a team's Claude Code setup gets more capable the longer it is used, not just faster.

You want it in chat apps and on a schedule. Telegram, Discord and iMessage alongside Slack, scheduled Routines, and remote control from a phone give Claude Code more places to plug into an existing workflow.

You are building a fleet of agents on Anthropic's stack. Subagents, background agents, and the Agent SDK are the pattern we actually run for clients, taking one terminal session to a small set of agents working a task list.

What we actually recommend

Pick the terminal agent that matches the subscription and ecosystem your team is already committed to, then evaluate it on your own codebase before rolling it out further. Both tools are credible, both ship real engineering, and both change fast enough that a comparison written today will need revisiting in a few months. If you are choosing cold, with no existing OpenAI or Anthropic footprint, our lean is Claude Code, because it is the tool we standardized on for client delivery and our CLAUDE.md, hooks and subagent setup is built around it. That is a statement about our workflow, not a claim that Codex CLI is worse at writing code.

If you want a second opinion in the same weight class, our Claude Code vs Cursor, Claude Code vs GitHub Copilot, and Claude vs ChatGPT for coding comparisons use the same verify-first approach. For a Codex-only primer, see what Codex CLI is and how to install it.

Picking a terminal agent is the easy part. The harder part is standing up CLAUDE.md conventions, permission policies, and multi-agent workflows that hold up in production, not just in a demo. That is the work we do daily for clients running Claude Code, and if you are new to the tool, our guide to setting up Claude Code is a good next step.

Frequently asked questions
Is OpenAI Codex CLI free?

Codex CLI itself is free, open source software. Using it requires either a ChatGPT plan or an API key billed at standard OpenAI API rates. OpenAI's pricing page lists Free ($0) and Go ($8/month) with GPT-6 Luna in the desktop app, subject to rollout, while Plus ($20/month) lists Codex in the CLI, IDE extension, web and iOS. There is no way to use Codex's model access entirely for free at unlimited volume.
Is Claude Code free?

The Claude Code client is free to install, but running it requires either a paid Claude subscription (Pro starts at $17-20/month) or an Anthropic Console account billed at API rates. Anthropic's free chat tier does not include Claude Code usage.
Which one is cheaper?

At the entry tier, they are effectively the same: $20/month gets you ChatGPT Plus with Codex access or Claude Pro with Claude Code access ($17/month if you pay Claude annually). Both top out their individual plans at "from $100/month" with a 5x-or-20x usage-multiplier structure. Actual cost depends far more on how much you use the tool and which model tier you run than on the plan sticker price.
Can I use Codex CLI and Claude Code together?

Yes. Nothing stops a team from running both, and some do, using whichever agent fits a given task or keeping both available for redundancy. They are separate tools with separate authentication, so there is no integration required to run them side by side.
Which one is open source?

Codex CLI is open source under the Apache-2.0 license. Claude Code is proprietary software from Anthropic, distributed as a client you install and authenticate against Anthropic's (or a Claude subscription's) backend.
Does either one require a developer to use safely?

Yes, both do. Both tools can edit files and run commands with varying levels of autonomy, and both rely on permission settings to control what happens without a human approving it first. Treat either one the way you would treat a junior engineer with shell access: review its output, do not grant broad autonomy in a production environment without guardrails, and keep a human in the loop for anything that touches deployment.
Which has more third-party model support?

Both can use more than one backend. OpenAI's docs say Codex can point at any model and provider that supports the Chat Completions or Responses APIs, with Chat Completions support deprecated. Claude Code's terminal CLI and VS Code extension support select third-party model providers alongside Anthropic's own models.
Which models does Codex CLI use in 2026?

OpenAI recommends GPT-6 Sol for complex coding and agentic work and GPT-6 Luna for focused, repeatable tasks, with GPT-6 Astra as its most capable model. GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna remain available during the rollout. GPT-5.5 retires from Codex with ChatGPT sign-in on October 14, 2026. Switch models with /model or codex --model.
Do Codex CLI and Claude Code both support MCP, hooks and subagents?

Yes. OpenAI's Codex docs cover MCP servers through codex mcp, hooks that run scripts or MCP tools during the agent loop, and subagents for splitting larger tasks. Claude Code has its own MCP support, hooks and subagents. The two differ in config files (AGENTS.md versus CLAUDE.md) and in the models behind them.
What are Codex CLI's sandbox and approval modes?

Codex combines a sandbox mode (read-only, workspace-write, or danger-full-access) with an approval policy such as on-request or never. In the Auto preset it edits and runs commands inside the working directory on its own and asks before touching files outside it or using the network. Change this with /permissions.

Running either agent inside a real engineering workflow (CI/CD, code review, migrations) is different from a solo trial. If you want help wiring Codex or Claude Code into your actual pipeline, see our Codex development agency. New to Codex specifically? See our how to use Codex walkthrough first.
